mechanism: Numeric MQTT v5 User Properties identify priorities. The modified non-preemptive broker transmission queue serves lower numeric priorities first, using FIFO within equal priority (Section 4.1). A UDP path serves time-critical traffic alongside conventional TCP clients.
model_assumptions: The decision acts in the broker forwarding/transmission path, not in downstream application processing. Priority metadata is supplied with messages. The evaluated configuration uses a particular industrial network, payload sizes and publication periods.
evidence_location: Table 3, PDF p. 8; Section 5.2 and Table 2, PDF p. 7; Section 5.1, PDF pp. 6-7
question_for_further_reading: Under identical transport and offered load, how much of the latency benefit remains attributable to dispatch order, and what happens to lower-priority traffic?

mechanism: Route classified messages into virtual queues and deliver to subscribers, with persistence for historical use. This is an architecture/classification intervention rather than an adaptive deadline or aging rule (architecture pp. 5-9).
model_assumptions: Messages are assigned to static Urgent, Critical and FCFS classes. The system uses MQTT-capable RabbitMQ/AMQP routing and MySQL persistence. The timing experiment is small.
evidence_location: PDF p. 10; Figs. 5-8, pp. 11-12; PDF p. 10; Figs. 3-4, PDF pp. 7-8
question_for_further_reading: How does static class prioritization affect tail waiting and delivery failures across classes as burst intensity rises?

decision_scope: Semantic alarm priority and source fairness
mechanism: Alarm=true maps to ALARM regardless of geography; routine traffic maps to HIGH/STANDARD/BACKGROUND. At completion, select the highest eligible band. Routine bands require tokens and rotate devices. With AAP deployed, ALARM rotates zones then devices in both inactive and active states (Eq. 16, p. 10); statically disabled AAP uses flat device RR. Active protection tests the per-source admission gate before the global gate (Eqs. 11-13, p. 9). Source rejection does not consume global tokens.
model_assumptions: Four strict priority bands share a non-preemptive local server. Alarm labels, geographic/device/source metadata and token parameters are available. The protected delay argument concerns admitted traffic under an arrival envelope and bounded blocking; it is not a path-wide guarantee.
evidence_location: Table 12, PDF p. 24, C3; Table 12, PDF p. 24, C3; Table 9, PDF p. 20, C2; Eq. 18, PDF p. 11
question_for_further_reading: Which routine-service tradeoffs remain when every comparator already recognizes semantic urgency and losses are measured over the full offered population?

mechanism: Model queue service as an RMAB, estimate transition matrices, compute state indices offline and select the highest-index queue at runtime. Algorithm 1 initializes index bounds to -1 and 3 and prints exact equality convergence conditions (manuscript p. 6 / PDF p. 8); numerical tolerances, caps and unseen-state handling need explicit implementation choices.
model_assumptions: Separate priority queues, slotted service and historical action-dependent transition information. The model discretizes occupancy to 21 levels and the priority-related occupancy ratio to six levels. Optimality claims rely on the cited RMAB/indexability/decoupling conditions.
evidence_location: Table IV, manuscript p. 9 / PDF p. 11; Section V-C, manuscript p. 9 / PDF p. 11; Section V, manuscript pp. 6-9 / PDF pp. 8-11
question_for_further_reading: How sensitive are the priority/congestion tradeoffs to transition-model mismatch, workload shifts and the cost of acquiring the learned state model?

mechanism: Allocate service using GRR with source sampling frequencies. Analyze the resulting peak-age violation probabilities under IPQ and SPQ; queue management affects whether old updates accumulate or are replaced.
model_assumptions: Periodic heterogeneous status updates, a shared base station and explicit queue-management models. Exponential/geometric service models enter the analysis. Freshness thresholds differ from deadlines attached to distinct emergency events.
evidence_location: Section V, Figs. 5-11, preprint pp. 21-25; Figs. 5-11, preprint pp. 22-25; Preprint p. 24
question_for_further_reading: When is an IoT item a replaceable state update rather than an event that must be retained, and how should that distinction constrain scheduling objectives?

mechanism: Reorder using deadline progress, migrate salvageable packets into fallback handling and choose next hops using congestion/history. The final combined Case 15 includes several interventions; its gain is not a queue-only effect.
model_assumptions: Clustered multi-hop WSN, priority classes, queue reordering, fallback migration and next-hop choice. Infinite queues remove overflow as a limiting factor (PDF p. 10); processing and topology assumptions further narrow the model.
evidence_location: PDF pp. 9-11; Conclusion, PDF p. 13; Discussion and Figs. 6-10, PDF p. 12
question_for_further_reading: What tradeoffs remain when resource capacity is bounded and routing, migration and scheduling effects are isolated?

mechanism: Analyze online fairness and packet-management policies, contrasting FCFS retention with replace-latest management. Compare RR, OTF, NMF, MITF and Random empirically; theorem conditions and stochastic simulations support different kinds of conclusions.
model_assumptions: A base station serves status updates for arriving/departing terminals. The legality of replacing old updates is central. Competitive analysis is worst-case relative to its own comparator/model, not an absolute emergency deadline guarantee.
evidence_location: Theorem 3 / Section 4; Theorems 15-16 / Section 6; Section 5, PDF p. 8; Section 5.5, PDF p. 9
question_for_further_reading: Which service guarantees are needed for non-replaceable alarms, and which failures remain hidden under ordinary stochastic workload averages?
